scenarios.title: My workplace is unsafe
scenarios.summary: Who takes a safety complaint depends on your state and on whether you work for a public or private employer. In Massachusetts, DLS covers public employers (the state's OSHA-approved plan for state and local government workers) and federal OSHA covers private ones. Elsewhere, 22 states and territories run their own OSHA-approved plan for both sectors, seven (Connecticut, Illinois, Maine, Massachusetts, New Jersey, New York and the Virgin Islands) cover public workers only, and some others, such as Ohio and Wisconsin, have their own public-employee safety laws. Ask your steward which office covers your workplace.
scenarios.urgency_text: Report a hazard promptly: federal OSHA cannot cite a violation more than six months old. Retaliation for raising safety has short deadlines: 30 days from when you are told of the action for an OSHA complaint, and a grievance does not pause it. For Massachusetts public employees: 30 days for a DLS complaint, six months for a DLR prohibited-practice charge, and two years for a c.149 s.185 lawsuit, which gives up the other routes.

concepts.name: Weingarten Rights
concepts.summary: An employee may ask for a union representative at an investigatory interview the employee reasonably believes will lead to discipline. The employer need not tell the employee about the right. A Massachusetts public employer that denies a valid request violates M.G.L. c. 150E, § 10(a)(1).
concepts.applies_to: Massachusetts public employees covered by M.G.L. c. 150E (the CERB follows the principles of NLRB v. J. Weingarten, Inc., 420 U.S. 251 (1975)), and union-represented private-sector employees under the NLRA.

concepts.name: Loudermill Due Process
concepts.summary: A tenured public employee is entitled to oral or written notice of the charges, an explanation of the employer's evidence, and an opportunity to respond before being discharged (Cleveland Bd. of Educ. v. Loudermill, 470 U.S. 532 (1985)). Massachusetts civil service law separately requires just cause, written notice, and a hearing for tenured civil service employees.
concepts.applies_to: Tenured public employees with a constitutionally protected property interest in their job; tenured Massachusetts civil service employees under M.G.L. c. 31, § 41.

concepts.name: Duty of Fair Representation
concepts.summary: A union must represent all bargaining-unit members without discrimination and regardless of membership. Under DLR precedent, a union breaches the duty if its conduct toward an employee is unlawfully motivated, arbitrary, perfunctory, or reflects inexcusable neglect; honest mistakes or simple negligence alone are not a breach.
concepts.applies_to: Every employee in a bargaining unit represented by an exclusive representative under M.G.L. c. 150E.

concepts.name: Past Practice
concepts.summary: In Massachusetts public employment, the employer's duty to bargain covers working conditions established through past practice as well as those in the contract. The DLR asks whether a practice is unequivocal, existed substantially unvaried for a reasonable period, and is known and accepted by both parties. Changing such a practice on a mandatory subject without notice and a chance to bargain can be a prohibited practice.
concepts.applies_to: Conditions of employment on mandatory subjects of bargaining, for example workload, job duties, payday schedules, and performance evaluation systems.

concepts.name: Cross-Statute Anti-Retaliation
concepts.summary: Many workplace laws separately prohibit retaliation for protected activity: filing or testifying under the public-sector bargaining law, workplace safety activity, wage complaints, PFML leave, discrimination complaints, and NLRB charges. Each has its own deadline; the shortest verified here is 30 days for public-sector safety retaliation.
concepts.applies_to: Workers who engaged in protected activity under the law in question.
